# 17-expanse — sources

Back-test entry `17-expanse.yaml`: Expanse, job sizes predicted at submit time on shared GPU clusters (YC Spring 2026,
P26). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named. "Author's
choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the Launch YC
post of 2026-05-04 and the Launch HN of 2026-06-01 (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later and sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Expanse - Unlock wasted GPU capacity", 2026-05-04 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/QCF-expanse-unlock-wasted-gpu-capacity
- [HN] Launch HN: "Launch HN: Expanse (YC P26) – Unlock Wasted GPU Capacity", 2026-06-01, the founders' post and the thread (27 comments), read whole through the HN Algolia API — https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48356312 (https://hn.algolia.com/api/v1/items/48356312)
- [WB] expanse.sh as archived 2026-06-01, the day of the Launch HN — https://web.archive.org/web/20260601142950/https://expanse.sh/
- [YCP] YC company page, read 2026-10-22 — https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/expanse
- [SITE] expanse.sh, read 2026-10-22 — https://expanse.sh

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Researchers and ML engineers who submit jobs to a shared SLURM or Kubernetes GPU cluster.
   [LYC] "Running compute on a cluster means guessing memory, time, and GPUs before you submit."
   [HN] "We also flag failures we think are about to happen and surface line-level optimisations the researcher can apply
   themselves." → `roles[researcher]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`.

2. **What (the job).** Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster.
   [LYC] "Get it wrong and your job fails mid-run. Over-guess and you pay for compute you never use."
   [HN] "under-requesting kills your job mid-run and you lose days of work. So everyone over-requests by two to three
   times." → `statements.problem`, `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** At every job submission. [HN] "We scan any workloads about to be submitted through SLURM/K8s
   (plugging into the life cycles of the job so you don't have to change how you submit things)". → `context.circumstance`,
   `occasion: job submission`. Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (several submissions a working day) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; Prevalence `p_80_100` ("everyone over-requests").

4. **Which people.** Researchers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100 or more GPUs, at national HPC centres, AI labs,
   quant funds and drug discovery.
   [HN] "If you run a HPC/GPU cluster (SLURM or K8s, 100+ GPUs), we'd love to have a talk." [LYC] "Know anyone in AI
   infrastructure (managing cloud and/or on-premise data centres), quant finance, drug discovery, or AI research labs?"
   → `context.segment`, `market: US`. Author's choice: US (rule U); the founders are in Edinburgh and the cluster they
   measured is a national-scale HPC site, and their ask names no country.

5. **Who pays.** The cluster's operator, per cluster; a department runs the paid pilot.
   [HN] "We offer a two-week measurement window where we install, ingest, and report recoverable capacity to datacenter
   operators, followed by a paid pilot deployment in one department at a fixed monthly fee, renewing at the same rate
   unless the scope expands." → `persona.decision_maker: {role: operator}`; Buyer and payer tests "The department head"
   (the author's reading of "in one department"), "The security team" listed. Purchase friction's tested item, "A security
   review of an agent on every node", from [HN] "Expanse installs on every node" and the thread's security objection
   ("Any competent enterprise risk team is going to give a hard no to a SaaS application being in the critical path for
   on-prem business critical workloads.") with the founder's reply ("Deployments are air-gapped and run in the customer's
   VPC, on their own hardware."); "Letting it read job scripts and source code" from [HN] "We read the source code, job
   submission script, and the hardware"; the budget line for the department's pilot is the author's. Commitment's step,
   "run a two-week waste measurement on the cluster": [WB] "Two weeks on your cluster. A real wastage number. No
   commitment. If the numbers don't justify a pilot, you walk away with the report." (The same post also offers "a
   section of your cluster for a week"; the two weeks of the pricing paragraph and the site are used.)

6. **Mechanism.** An agent on every node, hooked into the scheduler; a cluster-specific model predicts what each job needs
   at submit time.
   [HN] "Expanse installs on every node and hooks into SLURM (or the K8s scheduler). It ingests live hardware telemetry
   (DCGM, CUPTI, Cgroups, Network/IO monitoring)". [HN] "We predict the GPU VRAM, Utilisation, memory, CPUs and walltime
   the job actually needs, with a confidence interval." [HN] "If a workload fails, we take all the data we collected and
   perform correlations on the stack profiling and the hardware telemetry". [LYC] "All analysis runs on your network."
   → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`. Compatibility: the source code on the cluster beside the script
   (tested; the model reads it), the usual scheduler, Python ([HN] "currently only supported in python - other languages
   coming soon", of the profiler) — the conditions are the author's from these lines. Adoption friction: using the
   suggested sizes instead of padding (tested; [HN] "Our models are trained to over-provision rather than
   under-provision"), applying the code fixes. Relative advantage: [LYC] "Debug failures in seconds, not days"
   (fewer_attempts, the job runs first time) and a shorter queue wait for smaller requests (shorter_time, the author's
   reading of a smaller request fitting sooner); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** Per cluster a month, no figure; the cost is the share of the cluster's GPU hours reserved and
   never used.
   [HN] "We're currently onboarding customers as paid pilots. Pricing is determined per-cluster." No figure exists in
   [LYC], [HN], [WB] or [SITE] (no pricing page). The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a
   month**, is the operator's reading: for the smallest cluster the founders address (100 GPUs, about 73,000 GPU hours a
   month), [LYC]'s 30% reserved and unused is about 22,000 GPU hours, which at an assumed $2 to $3 a GPU hour (the
   author's assumption; [HN] prices its $8.5M "At on-demand cloud rates for the same hardware" without naming a rate) is
   about $44,000 to $66,000 a month; a fee of a fifth to a third of the waste on the smallest cluster is the author's
   choice. Existing sacrifice: RATE, about 30% to 59% of the cluster's GPU hours per cluster a month, the low from [LYC],
   the high from [HN]'s measured cluster. Ability to pay is read `budget` by the engine (a percent never compares with
   dollars), so the operators answer the registry's budget question.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from the thread; no respondent is a real person.
   [HN] (a genomics user) "I do genomics work and my jobs tend to be bursty. They may use a lot of CPU initially, but the
   second half of the job is writing results. This takes only one core, but still the max amount of memory." [HN] (an
   HPC user) "I know from snooping on sumbit scripts and node utilization on the HPC that I use at my institution that
   most submissions leave some compute on the table (and many of them are egregiously bad)." [HN] (a student) "It's not
   trivial to estimate a priori the amount of time required for my simulation to complete, so I overestimate."

- Gregory Lindqvist, Nadia Kowalski, Marco Bianchi → [HN] the measured national cluster and "Datacenters run at roughly 30% to 40% effective utilisation": operators who see the waste and would pay at the founder's band.
- Arjun Mehta → [HN] "large scale compute industries as well, such as quant funds": a quant-fund platform lead who owns the compute budget, sees more waste than the founder's high and decides alone (against the tested department head).

The split (4 of 7 operators at the founder's rung or above; 5 of 6 who give a number at 30% waste or more) is the
author's reading of a thread that agreed on the waste and argued about security and the business. No respondent
carries the name of a commenter, customer or founder.

## Status today

Same idea, five months after launch. [SITE] "Expanse delivers compute certainty. We predict exactly what every job
needs before it runs", still sales-led ("Book a discovery call"), now citing "$8M Monthly wastage uncovered" (a later
figure, not used). [YCP] lists the company as Spring 2026 with the Launch YC text. No public price today ([SITE] has no
pricing page, read 2026-10-22).

## Could not be sourced

- **A price figure.** None at launch or today; the founder's $10,000 to $20,000 per cluster a month is the operator's
  (author's) reading, and the GPU-hour rate behind its arithmetic is an assumption.
- **The waste per cluster as an operator would read it.** The founders' 30% is an industry figure they cite and their
  59% is one national cluster; the operators' value boxes (20% to 60%) are the author's.
- **A buyer title and who has to agree.** [HN] names "datacenter operators" and "one department"; the decider role, the
  department head as the tested role and the security team are the author's reading.
- **A US market.** The founders are in Edinburgh; the US is the author's choice under rule U.
- **A researcher's hour.** No source; `hourly_rate` 60 is a round stand-in, unread by the RATE cost.
- The Compatibility and Adoption friction conditions, the Purchase friction items but the security review, and every
  pick are the author's.

screens.why1: Right after I named the other hard parts at submit time, it makes sense to check the list strangers will hear and the belief it backs.
screens.why2: Memory, GPUs, run time, partition, queue and GPU-hour allocation are everyday words to any researcher on a SLURM or K8s cluster.
screens.why3: Every row is something a researcher does on their own cluster, so a stranger can answer from their last few submissions.
screens.why4: 'Moving data on and off the cluster' and 'Getting software working on the cluster' are real pains, but they happen before or after the moment a job is ready to submit, so they compete on a different occasion than the other rows.
screens.why5: These are the rows I typed and the belief repeats my own row word for word, so it still means what I meant.
screens.why7: The own row is on the list, first and locked, with four rivals and a belief that can go either way, but it restates the circumstance ('memory, GPUs and run time have to be guessed') instead of the part that goes wrong, no Check note flags this, and two rivals sit outside the submit moment.
screens.instead: Own: 'Sizing a job so it neither fails nor wastes GPUs'; rivals: 'Choosing which partition or queue to submit to' · 'Checking the group's GPU-hour allocation before submitting' · 'Writing the submission script for a new job' · 'Estimating how long the job will wait in the queue'

screens.why1: Reviewing my own difficulty and the rivals Keel kept or suggested, right after Save and before the stranger's version, is clearly where this check belongs.
screens.why2: Partition, queue, submit script, scheduler and GPU-hour allocation are everyday words to anyone running jobs on SLURM, so I read every row first time.
screens.why3: Each row is something my researchers do themselves at the moment a job goes in: sizing it, picking the partition, getting the script accepted, minding the allocation.
screens.why4: The own row only restates the circumstance ('have to be guessed first'), and 'Checking the group's allocation' is a quick lookup rather than something they want made easier, so two of four rows are weak, though none is nonsense or a duplicate.
screens.why5: My own row is word for word what I typed, but Keel's script-rejection row replaced one of mine and the screen shows neither which row it replaced ('In place of ...') nor my words behind Put back, so I can't see what drifted.
screens.why7: The rows share one measure, the count is right (own first plus three), and the belief can go either way with None of these on the stranger's side, but the own row breaks A3 by restating the circumstance instead of naming the part that goes wrong, which makes the belief near-tautological, and the replaced row lacks its 'In place of' line.
screens.instead: Sizing a job so it neither fails nor wastes GPUs (yours) · Choosing which partition or queue to submit to · Fixing submit scripts the scheduler rejects (in place of "<my original row>", Put back) · Fitting the run within the group's GPU-hour allocation

screens.why1: After the importance rows, asking how researchers size and submit jobs today is the obvious next step before testing whether that way falls short.
screens.why2: 'Get each job to run to the end without wasting the cluster' is my own phrasing of the job, and memory, GPUs and run time are everyday words on a SLURM cluster.
screens.why3: I know exactly how researchers pad their requests two to three times; we measured it across 122k jobs.
screens.why4: Two boxes plus the 'I'm not sure' escape is the right shape for a founder's answer, and the escape fits a founder who can't say.
screens.why5: Both boxes carry my words unchanged: guess then over-request two to three times, and my three rungs from sized right to three times or more.
screens.why7: My answer meets the card: the act and its means, plus three rungs on one measure (reserved versus used) with a working first rung; but the screen shows no prompt for the second box's other half, where 'good enough' ends, so the line falls to the default under the first rung without my placing it.
screens.instead: Keep the question; under the second box add: 'How did it go, best to worst, in your rungs, and which of them still counts as fine?' e.g. 'Ran first time, sized about right (fine) / Ran, holding about twice what it used'.

screens.why1: Right after I said how researchers size jobs today, checking the five outcomes that describe how that went is the natural next step.
screens.why2: 'Ran first time', 'holding three times what it used', 'failed partway and resubmitted' are exactly how anyone on a SLURM cluster talks about a job.
screens.why3: Every researcher knows from sacct or seff whether their last job ran, died, or sat on idle GPUs, so they can answer from their own last submission.
screens.why4: The five cover the real outcomes, but 'Failed partway and had to be resubmitted' and 'Never ran to the end' overlap for a job that died and was not yet rerun, and a job still queued or still running has no home.
screens.why5: The rungs are mine, but Keel's line under 'about twice' counts a 2x over-request as today's way working, when 'everyone over-requests by two to three times' is exactly the waste I'm selling against.
screens.why7: There is a working first rung, failure as the last rung, five in order, and the belief can go either way, but rung 4 grades failure rather than idle reservation, the very stand-in the card names, so the one-measure rule is bent.
screens.instead: Keep the five, move the line under 'Ran first time, sized about right', and reword rung 4 to 'Died partway; the whole reservation was wasted' so it stays on wasted GPU hours.

screens.why1: Saving my answers right before the study goes out to researchers is the obvious last step after checking what Keel wrote about the problem.
screens.why2: "Save your answers" is plain, but the pick "Lock and record the face Keel preselects" made me read it twice, because "face" is not a word I use and I had to guess it means the AI interviewer's look on the link.
screens.why3: Whether to save and lock my own answers before sending is entirely my own decision.

screens.why1: Choosing how the link reaches researchers is the natural last step once the problem study is saved and before it goes out.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits under the title with 'Frequency: 4 counted' beside it, and the card spells out 4 counted against 5 needed, so I know the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: There is no chart here, only the tally '4 beliefs: 1 holding · 3 too few to call · 7 people answered' and per-card counts like '6 of 7 said yes · bar 6 of 7', and I read who was counted, out of how many, and where each bar sits on first look.
screens.why_b3: Importance and Current solution are my belief about guessing sizes at submit, but Prevalence and Frequency make the occasion 'a job fail mid-run', which is the rare under-request case; my point is that everyone over-requests at every submission precisely so jobs don't fail.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the page says what to do: not to get more researchers past the 5 needed, nor what 'Holding up' on Prevalence means for Expanse.
screens.why_b5: n is visible and three cards honestly say too few to call, but Prevalence is called 'Holding up' at exactly the bar on 7 people with no word that 7 is a small sample.
screens.instead: Too few to call: 3 of 4 beliefs had only 4 researchers counted where 5 are needed, so send the study to more researchers; prevalence held at 6 of 7, just at the bar on a small sample, and it should ask about over-requesting at submit, not jobs failing mid-run.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Holding up' sits right beside the number that decides it, 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 6 of 7, so I know it held and exactly why: at the edge, not above it.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 7 people on a 0-to-7 axis, 6 for and 1 against, with my bar marked at 6, so what is counted, out of how many, and where the bar sits are all plain at first look.
screens.why_b3: I recognise it, but my segment was researchers and ML engineers on SLURM or Kubernetes clusters of 100+ GPUs and the card drops that qualifier. The event 'had a job fail mid-run' is also only the under-request side of my problem; the waste from everyone padding two to three times is what I'd sell on.
screens.why_b4: The So line only points to the next two cards. It doesn't say what a bare pass at exactly my bar means for me, such as that one more No among seven would have sunk it, so lean on Frequency and Importance before trusting it.
screens.why_b5: n=7 stays visible, the count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and the So line says 'at your bar exactly' rather than calling it strong. The stray '— the most recent time it happened' tacked onto a yes/no gate is clutter, not an overclaim.
screens.instead: Holding up, just: 6 of 7 researchers on 100+ GPU SLURM/K8s clusters had a job fail mid-run, exactly your 8-in-10 bar, so one more No would have sunk it; treat it as a lean and check how often it bites and what it costs on the next two cards.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside its deciding number, '4 counted · 5 needed to call it', and the So line repeats both, so I know the answer and why at once.

screens.why1: As the first screen, it plainly checks whether I'm on the kind of big shared GPU cluster the study is about, so it's obvious why it's asked.
screens.why2: Running jobs on a cluster and counting it in GPUs is how I talk about my work every day, so I can answer at first hearing.
screens.why3: I know roughly how big our cluster is, since I see it in sinfo and in the queue, so I can answer from what I know; someone on a borderline cluster might have to guess.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly for a gate, and leaving out an escape is right for a screener.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's segment of clusters of 100 or more GPUs without hinting at any product, though it drops 'shared' and 'SLURM or Kubernetes', so someone with a private 100-GPU cluster also gets through.
screens.why6: It's one short question and easy to answer once heard, though 'I'll read 2 options. Yes; or No.' is stiffer than a plain 'Yes or no.'
screens.instead: Do you submit jobs to a shared cluster with 100 or more GPUs, on SLURM or Kubernetes? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming I'm on a 100+ GPU cluster, asking whether a job died on me this week is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: "Job fail mid-run" is how I'd say it myself; nothing here I'd have to read twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly which of my jobs died in the last week, so I can answer from memory.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it cleanly, and the story-box chips aren't the gate's to answer for.
screens.why5: "Fail" covers any death, including a NaN, a bug in my code or a bad node, so it drifts a little from a job killed for under-requesting memory or time, though nothing of a product leaks.
screens.why6: One short question and "Yes or no" is easy to hold and answer on one hearing.
screens.why7: There are two fixed answers and no escape, and the event is a costly act some of us truly didn't have this week, so the share can support or refute the band.
screens.instead: In the last 5 working days, did you have a job killed mid-run? Yes · No

screens.why1: I just said yes, a job of mine failed mid-run this week, so asking on how many days that happened is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: 'Job', 'fail mid-run' and 'working days' are exactly how I'd say it about my SLURM runs, and I can answer on first read.
screens.why3: I know which days this week a run died partway, whether from an OOM, a time-limit kill or a crash, because I lost the work each time.
screens.why4: One button for each of the five days is complete and distinct, and 'I can't recall' fits when I've had a lot of jobs going.
screens.why5: It asks about my own failed jobs in plain trade words, with nothing about a product, a company or how the founder labels people like me.
screens.why6: Heard once it's short and holds: one question, 'a number from 1 to 5', then the can't-recall escape.
screens.why7: Every option is a count of working days from 1 to the window's 5 with no 0 or bands, the unit is said once, the clause is six words, the escape is present and apart, and the founder's range isn't shown here to fault the balance.

screens.why1: After asking about jobs failing mid-run, it makes sense to ask which part of getting a job onto the cluster I would most like made easier.
screens.why2: Partition, queue, GPU-hour allocation and the scheduler rejecting a submit script are everyday words for me on a shared SLURM cluster.
screens.why3: I do every one of these myself each time I submit, so I can answer from my last run without guessing.
screens.why4: The four options are distinct parts of my own submit step, none holds another, and None of these fits as the way out.
screens.why5: Nothing of a product reaches me; the founder's guessing of memory, GPUs and run time is kept in plain words.
screens.why6: It says well overall, but the own option is itself a three-item list and partition or queue adds another pair, so the list is harder to hold by ear.
screens.why7: The own row is present, never first, with three rivals and the None of these escape at the first ask, but it packs three things into one option, which bends the one-thing rule.
screens.instead: Think of your last run of jobs on the cluster. Which one of these would you most like made easier? Sizing a job's memory and GPUs before submitting; Checking the group's GPU-hour allocation before submitting; Fixing submit scripts the scheduler rejects; Choosing which partition to submit to; or None of these.

screens.why1: Right after picking out guessing my job's resources as the pain, asking how my last submission's sizing actually went is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: I'd say 'requesting' or 'sizing' rather than 'guessing ... go', 'a job' repeats 'job submission', and 'holding' isn't how I'd describe what I asked for versus what it used.
screens.why3: I can pull what my last job used from seff or sacct, but 'twice what it used' lumps memory, time and GPUs together, and they're rarely over by the same amount, so I'd be guessing which one to answer for.
screens.why4: 'Failed partway and had to be resubmitted' and 'Never ran to the end' overlap for a job that died and was rerun, and there's no clear rung for the 1.5x case between 'about right' and 'about twice'.
screens.why5: Nothing of the product or the founder's terms reaches me; it's about my own job sizing.
screens.why6: It says mostly well, but 'how did guessing memory, time and GPUs before submitting a job go' is clumsy heard once, and 'ran, holding three times or more what it used' is a mouthful.
screens.why7: There is a working rung first, a line can sit under it, the order runs best to worst and the one escape fits, but 'Failed partway and had to be resubmitted' switches from how much idle reservation I held to whether the job ran, which the card names as off the measure.
screens.instead: Think of the last job you submitted. How did what you requested compare with what it used? Requested about what it used · Requested up to twice what it used · Requested over twice what it used · Requested too little, so it was killed · Never got it sized right to finish — or say you can't recall.
